items.title: AlexNet Should Never Have Worked (Simon Prince)
items.summary: Simon Prince on why AlexNet should never have worked. It had 60 million parameters, orders of magnitude more than the vision models of its time. Simon Prince is the author of Understanding Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2023). #Shorts #deeplearning #AlexNet #machinelearning Watch the full conversation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sJXn4Cl4oww

items.title: Does Gen Z Actually Hate AI?
items.summary: Ad executives guessed how young people feel about AI-made ads: 82% thought Gen Z and millennials felt positive, but only 45% did (IAB). Gallup found the youngest adults the most negative of any age, mostly fine with AI for brainstorming but hardest on AI-made faces and voices. Older people aren't fans either. With younger customers, a shaky video of your real trainer could beat a perfect fake.

items.title: AlphaGenome 2: Teaching AI to read the entire human genome
items.summary: 98% of human DNA doesn't build proteins—it controls how our cells work, and holds vital clues to why diseases happen and why 90% of new drugs fail in clinical trials. Understanding the genome at the molecular level is the key to deciphering the blueprint of human life. In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry speaks with Google DeepMind's Žiga Avsec and Adam Gayoso about AlphaGenome, the AlphaGenome Atlas, and AlphaGenome 2—exploring how AI reads non-coding DNA down to single-cell resolution to pinpoint disease-causing mutations and help researchers solve medical mysteries. items.title: Claude's "Clean-Room" Compiler Copied LLVM's Mistakes (Jeremy Howard)
items.summary: Jeremy Howard, co-founder of fast.ai and Answer.AI, on Anthropic's "clean-room" C compiler written by Claude. Chris Lattner's LLVM, the most widely used foundation for compilers, is in the training data many times over, so converting it to Rust is an interpolation between parts of that data: a style-transfer problem. The giveaway is that it copied parts of LLVM that Chris now says were a mistake. In Jeremy's words: "That doesn't happen accidentally. That happens because you're not actually being creative." items.title: Random Code Starts Copying Itself (Blaise Agüera y Arcas)
items.summary: Blaise Agüera y Arcas on the BFF experiment. Start with a soup of 1,024 tapes, each 64 random bytes. Pluck two at random, join them end to end, run them, pull them apart, put them back, and repeat. That's the entire experiment. Out of it come complex programs that copy themselves and each other: in his words, "emergence of life in this very functional minimal sense from randomness."
